---
title: "Expected Returns"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Expected Returns"
  description-meta: "Where the expected-return vector comes from and how imprecisely it is known: the standard error of a mean, Bayes-Stein shrinkage, and equilibrium returns by reverse optimization, implemented in R with PortfolioAnalytics."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

Every optimizer in this book consumes a vector of expected returns, and nothing
in the data pins that vector down as well as the covariance matrix beside it.
@merton1980 established why: the standard error of a mean estimated over a span
of $\tau$ years is $\sigma/\sqrt{\tau}$ whatever the sampling frequency, so
only a longer history helps, and thirty years of it leaves an annual risk
premium known to within several percentage points. That is a property of the
object rather than of any estimator, and it is the reason expected returns are
the hard input of @sec-09-mean-variance-theory while the covariance matrix of
@sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory is merely a large one.

This chapter is about **strategic** expected returns in the sense of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: the unconditional vector
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ a long-run policy is set on, with no information about where
in the cycle we stand. Conditional forecasts are the tactical work of
@sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-theory, and turning an opinion into a return is
the subject of @sec-17-expressing-views-theory. We first measure how imprecisely
each of the sixteen means is known and what that does to a return target, then
set out the two alternatives to the sample mean, shrinkage toward a common
value and reverse optimization from market weights, then implement both and
show how `PortfolioAnalytics` takes a mean vector it did not compute, and
finally feed the three vectors to the same tangency problem to see what each
buys and how much each moves when the sample changes.

The data are the sixteen risky class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, in excess of the Treasury bill for
the reasons given in @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory.

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
N <- ncol(Re); T <- nrow(Re); years <- T / 12
```

## How Precisely a Mean Can Be Known {#sec-06-expected-returns-theory}

Write $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ for the vector of sample means of the excess
returns and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ for their sample covariance, as in
@sec-09-mean-variance-theory. Each element of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ is an
average of $T$ monthly observations, and if those observations are independent
with volatility $\sigma$ per year, the standard error of the annualized mean is

$$
\operatorname{se}(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}},
$$ {#eq-06-se}

where $\tau$ is the calendar span in years. @eq-04-precision derived this
alongside the standard error of the variance, and the contrast between the two
is the point of @merton1980: the sampling interval does not appear in
@eq-06-se, so nothing short of more calendar time improves it. A 95 percent
interval for the mean is

$$
\hat{\mu} \pm 1.96\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}},
$$ {#eq-06-interval}

and setting its half-width equal to the mean itself gives the span of history
needed before the interval excludes zero:

$$
\tau^{*} = \left(\frac{1.96\,\sigma}{\mu}\right)^{2}.
$$ {#eq-06-years}

Both quantities are computable for every series, and the table they produce is
the right way to begin a chapter on expected returns.

```{r}
#| label: precision
mu_s <- colMeans(Re)                 # monthly sample means, the mu of chapter 9
S    <- stats::cov(Re)               # the sample covariance of chapter 7

precision <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = colnames(Re),
  mean  = mu_s * 12,
  vol   = apply(Re, 2, stats::sd) * sqrt(12)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(se    = vol / sqrt(years),                 # @eq-06-se
                t     = mean / se,
                lower = mean - 1.96 * se,                  # @eq-06-interval
                upper = mean + 1.96 * se,
                years_needed = (1.96 * vol / mean)^2) |>   # @eq-06-years
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(t))

n_straddle <- sum(precision$lower < 0)
c(series = nrow(precision), interval_includes_zero = n_straddle,
  median_se = median(precision$se), median_years_needed = median(precision$years_needed))
```

```{r}
#| label: precision-picks
#| include: false
us <- precision[precision$asset == "US_equity", ]
lo <- precision[nrow(precision), ]
# The text takes US_equity as the best case and the last row as the worst.
stopifnot(identical(precision$asset[1], "US_equity"), us$lower > 0,
          lo$t == min(precision$t), lo$lower < 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-06-precision
#| tbl-cap: "The sixteen annualized mean excess returns with their standard errors from @eq-06-se, the 95 percent interval of @eq-06-interval, and the years of history @eq-06-years says would be needed for that interval to exclude zero. Sorted by t-statistic."
#| echo: false
precision |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(mean, vol, se, lower, upper), ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * .x)),
                t = sprintf("%.2f", t),
                years_needed = sprintf("%.0f", years_needed)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "mean", "volatility", "std. error", "t",
                      "lower", "upper", "years to exclude zero"))
```

Take the series whose mean is furthest from zero relative to its standard
error, `r us$asset`. Its annualized volatility is `r sprintf("%.3f", us$vol)` and the sample spans
`r years` model years, so by @eq-06-se

$$
\operatorname{se}(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{`r sprintf("%.3f", us$vol)`}{\sqrt{`r years`}}
= `r sprintf("%.4f", us$se)`,
$$

a standard error of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * us$se)` percentage points on a
mean of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * us$mean)`, and an interval from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * us$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * us$upper)`.
That is the best case. For `r n_straddle` of the `r nrow(precision)` series
the interval of @eq-06-interval includes zero: the data do not reject the
hypothesis that the asset carries no risk premium at all. The median series
would need `r sprintf("%.0f", median(precision$years_needed))` years of history
before it did, and `r lo$asset`, with a mean of
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * lo$mean)` against a standard error of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * lo$se)` points, would need
`r sprintf("%.0f", lo$years_needed)`. @fama2002 make the same point on a
century and a quarter of United States data: the realized equity premium is
estimated with a standard error that leaves its level open to debate by several
percentage points, which is why they estimate it from dividend and earnings
growth instead. @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation measured the
practical counterpart on this market, a rolling sixty-month mean that wanders
by more than its own level, and @fig-04-instability shows it. Nothing in this
chapter improves on @eq-06-se; the estimators below manage the imprecision
rather than remove it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Sampling more finely helps the variance and not the mean

The obvious response to an imprecise mean is more observations, and the weekly
panel `sim_class_returns_weekly` holds the same `r years` model years at more
than four times the resolution. @eq-04-precision says what to expect: the
standard error of the variance falls with $\sqrt{T}$, and the standard error
of the mean does not move.

```{r}
#| label: frequency
Rw   <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_weekly, date, class, return)
# The weekly bill series starts one week before the return panel: align by date.
rf_w <- sim_riskfree_weekly$return[match(zoo::index(Rw), sim_riskfree_weekly$date)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(rf_w), identical(colnames(Rw), colnames(Re)))
Rew  <- Rw - rf_w

freq <- tibble::tibble(
  asset     = colnames(Re),
  se_mean_m = apply(Re,  2, stats::sd) * sqrt(12) / sqrt(nrow(Re) / 12),
  se_mean_w = apply(Rew, 2, stats::sd) * sqrt(52) / sqrt(nrow(Rew) / 52),
  se_var_m  = apply(Re,  2, stats::var) * 12 * sqrt(2 / nrow(Re)),
  se_var_w  = apply(Rew, 2, stats::var) * 52 * sqrt(2 / nrow(Rew))
)
c(months = nrow(Re), weeks = nrow(Rew),
  mean_se_ratio     = median(freq$se_mean_w / freq$se_mean_m),
  variance_se_ratio = median(freq$se_var_w / freq$se_var_m),
  sqrt_T_ratio      = sqrt(nrow(Re) / nrow(Rew)))
```

Going from `r nrow(Re)` months to `r nrow(Rew)` weeks leaves the standard
error of the mean where it was, at a median ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", median(freq$se_mean_w / freq$se_mean_m))`, and cuts the
standard error of the variance to
`r sprintf("%.2f", median(freq$se_var_w / freq$se_var_m))` of its monthly
value, against the `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(nrow(Re) / nrow(Rew)))` that
$\sqrt{T}$ predicts. This is why @sec-07-covariance-matrix-implementation can
estimate its input from the same history that leaves this chapter's input
undetermined.
:::

### A target set on a sample mean

@eq-09-problem fixes a return target $\bar{\mu}$ and asks for the least
variance that attains it, and @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation solves that
program with $\bar{\mu}$ set at the upper quartile of the sample means. The
constraint $\boldsymbol{w}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \bar{\mu}$ is then satisfied
to the solver's tolerance, on an input known to the precision of
@tbl-06-precision.

```{r}
#| label: target
target_m <- as.numeric(quantile(mu_s, 0.75))      # the target chapter 9 imposes
se_med   <- median(precision$se)
c(target_annual = target_m * 12, median_se = se_med,
  target_lower = target_m * 12 - 1.96 * se_med,
  target_upper = target_m * 12 + 1.96 * se_med)
```

The target is `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * target_m * 12)` a year, held to eight
decimal places. The inputs that define it carry a median standard error of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * se_med)` percentage points, so a mean of that size is
itself known only to somewhere between
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (target_m * 12 - 1.96 * se_med))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (target_m * 12 + 1.96 * se_med))`. A constraint set
on a sample mean is a constraint set on noise, and the optimizer honors it
exactly.

The literature on what follows is old and consistent, and one sentence each
suffices here because @sec-09-mean-variance-theory has already used it.
@jobson1980 showed that the sampling distribution of the estimated tangency
weights is so wide that the portfolio's expected Sharpe ratio falls far short
of the one the estimate promises. @best1991 traced the mechanism to
@eq-09-tangency: the weights are $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}$ applied to
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, so an error in a mean is magnified by the condition
number of the covariance matrix on its way into the portfolio. @chopra1993
priced the two inputs against each other and found errors in means roughly an
order of magnitude more costly than errors in variances. @michaud1989 named the
consequence, an optimizer that systematically overweights whatever the sample
flattered. @kan2007 derived the expected out-of-sample loss of the plug-in
rule, showed that the term due to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ dominates, and
proposed holding the sample tangency portfolio alongside the minimum-variance
portfolio of @eq-09-gmv, which is exactly what the shrinkage estimator below
turns out to do. @demiguel2009 supplied the empirical verdict with fourteen
rules on seven datasets: none that estimates the mean was consistently better
than equal weighting out of sample. @sec-08-estimation-error-theory measures
the cost on this market and @sec-26-forecast-error-cost-theory derives it.

### Shrinkage of the mean

The response from statistics predates all of that. @stein1956 showed that for
three or more means estimated jointly, the vector of sample means is
inadmissible under quadratic loss: an estimator that pulls every element
toward a common value has lower expected error whatever the true means are.
@james1961 gave the estimator its form, a shrinkage factor that depends on how
far the sample means sit from their target, and @efron1975 the intuition, that
a set of estimates spread by sampling error is always spread too far.
@jorion1985 brought the argument to portfolios and @jorion1986 gave it the
form that is still used. The target is the expected return of the
minimum-variance portfolio, the one number about $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ that
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ alone pins down, and the estimator is

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\text{BS}}
= (1-v)\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} + v\,\mu_0\,\boldsymbol{\iota},
\qquad
\mu_0 = \frac{\boldsymbol{\iota}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}
             {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}},
\qquad
v = \frac{N+2}
         {(N+2) + T\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\mu_0\boldsymbol{\iota})'
                     \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}
                     (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\mu_0\boldsymbol{\iota})}.
$$ {#eq-06-bayes-stein}

The intensity $v$ is set by the data rather than chosen. The quadratic form in
its denominator is $T$ times the squared distance of the sample means from
their target, measured in the metric of the covariance matrix; when the means
are far apart relative to their sampling error, $v$ is small and the sample is
trusted, and when they are indistinguishable, $v$ approaches one and every
asset is assigned the same expected return. As $T$ grows, $v$ falls to zero,
so the estimator is consistent. This is the same construction as
@eq-07-shrinkage for the covariance matrix, where @ledoit2004 derive the
analogous intensity, and it has the same character: a biased estimator with
lower total error than the unbiased one.

What shrinkage does to the portfolio is visible from @eq-09-tangency. Because
the map from means to unconstrained tangency weights is linear,

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\text{BS}}
= (1-v)\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
+ v\,\mu_0\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota},
$$ {#eq-06-bs-direction}

a combination of the sample tangency direction and the minimum-variance
direction of @eq-09-gmv. Shrinking the means toward $\mu_0$ therefore moves
the tangency portfolio toward the minimum-variance portfolio, which is the
three-fund rule of @kan2007 arrived at from the estimator's side. Other targets
are possible and each carries an argument: @pastor2000 and @mackinlay2000
shrink toward the means a factor model such as that of
@sec-05-factor-models-implementation implies, @tu2011 combine the sample rule
with equal weighting, and @garlappi2007 reach a shrinkage form from ambiguity
aversion rather than from loss. The target used here is the one that needs no
model beyond $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$.

### Equilibrium returns by reverse optimization

The third route asks a different question. Rather than estimating
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ from the history of returns, it asks what
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ would have to be for a portfolio someone actually holds to
be optimal. @sharpe1974 posed the problem in that form, and @black1992 chose
the portfolio: the market, weighted by capitalization, which is the portfolio
the equilibrium of @sharpe1964 and @lintner1965 says every investor holds.
An investor who maximizes
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\delta}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$
has the first-order condition
$\boldsymbol{\mu} = \delta\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$, derived in
@sec-91-proofs-quadratic-utility, and if the aggregate investor holds the
market, the expected returns consistent with that are

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}} = \delta\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}.
$$ {#eq-06-equilibrium}

The scalar $\delta$ is the market's risk aversion, and premultiplying
@eq-06-equilibrium by $\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'$ shows how to read it from
the market's own history:

$$
\delta = \frac{\mu_{\text{mkt}}}{\sigma^{2}_{\text{mkt}}}
       = \frac{\text{SR}_{\text{mkt}}}{\sigma_{\text{mkt}}},
$$ {#eq-06-delta}

the market's expected excess return divided by its variance, which is the same
number whether computed from monthly or from annual moments. @he1999 give the
intuition for what the resulting vector does inside an optimizer,
@satchell2000 the Bayesian derivation, and @idzorek2007 a step-by-step
account of the full model with views attached; the views are
@sec-17-expressing-views-theory's subject, and only the prior is used here.

Three properties of @eq-06-equilibrium matter here. It is not a forecast: it
is the vector for which the market portfolio is the tangency portfolio of
@eq-09-tangency, by construction, so an optimizer handed
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ returns
$\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}$, a portfolio that is held, diversified and
consistent with the covariance matrix. $\delta$ scales every element alike,
and the tangency portfolio is invariant to scale, so $\delta$ sets how much of
the portfolio is risky rather than what the risky part holds; it matters for
position size and, in @sec-17-expressing-views-theory, for how heavily a view
is weighed against the prior. And the package's `risk_aversion` argument is
$\gamma/2$ in the notation of @sec-91-proofs-quadratic-utility, so reproducing
the market portfolio requires `risk_aversion` set to $\delta/2$, verified
numerically below.

The weakness of the method is the weight vector. @roll1977 is the reminder that
the market portfolio is not observable, and on this market the problem is
concrete: `sim_marketcap_weekly` carries capitalizations for the
`r sum(sim_assets$asset_class == "equity")` equity instruments and for nothing
else. No capitalization exists for the government or credit series or for the
commodity index, so a full class-level equilibrium cannot be read from the data
as shipped. We do the two things that can be done: a clean demonstration on the
five equity classes, whose weights are their capitalizations, and a class-level
version on a stated proxy for the rest, kept in a box and labelled as the
assumption it is.

## Three Estimators in Code {#sec-06-expected-returns-implementation}

### Bayes-Stein in a few lines

@eq-06-bayes-stein is a function of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$,
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, $N$ and $T$, and nothing else. @jorion1986 scales
the sample covariance by $(T-1)/(T-N-2)$ before inverting it, which makes the
inverse unbiased; on `r T` observations and `r N` assets the factor is
`r sprintf("%.3f", (T - 1) / (T - N - 2))` and changes $v$ at the second
decimal.

```{r}
#| label: bayes-stein
bayes_stein <- function(R) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu   <- colMeans(X)
  S    <- stats::cov(X) * (T - 1) / (T - N - 2)   # Jorion's unbiased scaling
  Sinv <- solve(S); iota <- rep(1, N)
  mu0  <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% mu) / as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% iota)
  d    <- mu - mu0
  v    <- (N + 2) / ((N + 2) + T * as.numeric(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d))
  list(mu = setNames((1 - v) * mu + v * mu0, colnames(X)), mu0 = mu0, v = v)
}

bs <- bayes_stein(Re)
stopifnot(bs$v > 0.5, bs$v < 0.6)    # "more than half" and "roughly halved" below
c(v = bs$v, mu0_annual = bs$mu0 * 12)
```

The intensity is $v = `r sprintf("%.3f", bs$v)`$ and the target is
$\mu_0 = `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * bs$mu0 * 12)`$ a year, the expected return
of the minimum-variance portfolio. For `r us$asset` the estimator of
@eq-06-bayes-stein reads

$$
\hat{\mu}_{\text{BS}}
= (1 - `r sprintf("%.3f", bs$v)`) \times `r sprintf("%.4f", us$mean)`
+ `r sprintf("%.3f", bs$v)` \times `r sprintf("%.4f", bs$mu0 * 12)`
= `r sprintf("%.4f", bs$mu[[us$asset]] * 12)`,
$$

so more than half of the distance between the sample mean and the common value
is removed. The same happens to every series, in both directions.

```{r}
#| label: shrinkage-frame
mu_long <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = rep(colnames(Re), 2),
  kind  = rep(c("sample mean", "Bayes-Stein"), each = N),
  value = c(mu_s, bs$mu) * 12
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(asset = factor(asset, levels = names(sort(mu_s))))
stopifnot(nrow(mu_long) == 2 * N, !anyNA(mu_long$value))

# The ordering is untouched: the same ranks, asset by asset.
stopifnot(identical(names(mu_s), names(bs$mu)), identical(rank(mu_s), rank(bs$mu)))
c(spread_sample = diff(range(mu_s)) * 12, spread_shrunk = diff(range(bs$mu)) * 12,
  rank_correlation = stats::cor(mu_s, bs$mu, method = "spearman"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-06-shrinkage
#| fig-cap: "Sample means and Bayes-Stein estimates for the sixteen series, annualized. Each segment joins an asset's two estimates; the dashed line is the common target, the expected return of the minimum-variance portfolio. The ordering is untouched and the spread is roughly halved."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.7
mu_long |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(value, asset)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = bs$mu0 * 12, linetype = "22",
                      colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(group = asset), colour = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]],
                     linewidth = 1.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = kind), size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "annualized expected excess return", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

The spread between the highest and the lowest expected return falls from
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * diff(range(mu_s)) * 12)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * diff(range(bs$mu)) * 12)` percentage points, and the
rank correlation between the two vectors is
`r sprintf("%.2f", stats::cor(mu_s, bs$mu, method = "spearman"))`, because
@eq-06-bayes-stein is a linear map with a positive slope. Shrinkage changes
how different the assets look, not which looks better.

### Equilibrium returns for the five equity classes

The clean case first. Each regional equity class is the capitalization-weighted
sum of its instruments, so its weight in the world equity market is the sum of
their capitalizations. As in @sec-05-factor-models-implementation the weight
used in month $t$ is the last one observed on or before the end of month
$t-1$, a weight that could have been held.

```{r}
#| label: market-weights-equity
eq_ids     <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
region_of  <- setNames(sim_assets$region, sim_assets$asset_id)
eq_classes <- grep("_equity$", colnames(Re), value = TRUE)

# Capitalization of each region's listed equities, week by week.
cap_region <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% eq_ids) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = paste0(region_of[asset], "_equity")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(cap = sum(market_cap), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = class, values_from = cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
stopifnot(setequal(setdiff(names(cap_region), "date"), eq_classes), !anyNA(cap_region))
cap_mat <- as.matrix(cap_region[, eq_classes])      # columns in class order, by name

d <- zoo::index(Re)
W_eq <- t(vapply(seq_along(d), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) d[1] - 31 else d[i - 1]     # last week of the previous month
  j <- max(which(cap_region$date <= cutoff))
  cap_mat[j, ] / sum(cap_mat[j, ])
}, numeric(length(eq_classes))))
colnames(W_eq) <- eq_classes
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W_eq) - 1) < 1e-10), identical(colnames(W_eq), eq_classes))

round(rbind(first = W_eq[1, ], average = colMeans(W_eq), last = W_eq[nrow(W_eq), ]), 3)
```

The composition drifts, from `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * W_eq[1, "US_equity"])`
United States at the start to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * W_eq[nrow(W_eq), "US_equity"])` at the end, which
@sec-05-factor-models-implementation found for the same proxy. An
unconditional $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is matched to an unconditional weight vector,
so we use the average composition over the sample; the last month's weights are
an exercise. The market's own excess return calibrates $\delta$ through
@eq-06-delta.

```{r}
#| label: equilibrium-equity
mkt_e  <- rowSums(W_eq * zoo::coredata(Re[, eq_classes]))   # the market's excess return
delta  <- mean(mkt_e) / stats::var(mkt_e)                    # @eq-06-delta
w_mkt5 <- colMeans(W_eq)
S5     <- S[eq_classes, eq_classes]
mu_eq5 <- setNames(delta * as.numeric(S5 %*% w_mkt5), eq_classes)   # @eq-06-equilibrium
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_mkt5 * mu_eq5) - delta * as.numeric(t(w_mkt5) %*% S5 %*% w_mkt5)) < 1e-12)

c(market_return = mean(mkt_e) * 12, market_vol = stats::sd(mkt_e) * sqrt(12),
  market_sharpe = mean(mkt_e) / stats::sd(mkt_e) * sqrt(12), delta = delta)
```

With an annualized excess return of `r sprintf("%.4f", mean(mkt_e) * 12)` and a
variance of `r sprintf("%.4f", stats::var(mkt_e) * 12)`, @eq-06-delta gives

$$
\delta = \frac{`r sprintf("%.4f", mean(mkt_e) * 12)`}{`r sprintf("%.4f", stats::var(mkt_e) * 12)`}
= `r sprintf("%.2f", delta)`,
$$

and @eq-06-equilibrium then produces one expected return per class.

```{r}
#| label: equity-comparison
prem_eq <- sum(w_mkt5 * mu_eq5)               # the market's own equilibrium premium
beta5   <- mu_eq5 / prem_eq                     # (Sigma w) / (w' Sigma w), asset by asset

cmp5 <- tibble::tibble(
  asset       = eq_classes,
  weight      = w_mkt5,
  beta        = beta5,
  sample      = mu_s[eq_classes] * 12,
  se          = precision$se[match(eq_classes, precision$asset)],
  equilibrium = mu_eq5 * 12
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap_in_se = (equilibrium - sample) / se)
stopifnot(identical(cmp5$asset, eq_classes), !anyNA(cmp5),
          abs(sum(w_mkt5 * beta5) - 1) < 1e-12)
# The two revisions the text reads off the table: JP_equity up, US_equity down.
stopifnot(cmp5$gap_in_se[cmp5$asset == "JP_equity"] > 0,
          cmp5$gap_in_se[cmp5$asset == "US_equity"] < 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-06-equilibrium-equity
#| tbl-cap: "Sample means and equilibrium returns for the five equity classes, annualized. Beta is the class's beta on the market portfolio; the last column is the gap between the two estimates in units of the sample mean's standard error."
#| echo: false
cmp5 |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(weight, sample, se, equilibrium), ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * .x)),
                beta = sprintf("%.2f", beta),
                gap_in_se = sprintf("%+.2f", gap_in_se)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "market weight", "beta", "sample mean", "std. error",
                      "equilibrium", "gap, in std. errors"))
```

Dividing @eq-06-equilibrium by the market's own equilibrium premium
$\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}$ shows what the
vector is: each element is the asset's beta on the market times that premium,

$$
\mu_{\text{eq},i}
= \frac{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}})_i}
       {\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}}
  \times \boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}
= \beta_i \times `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * prem_eq * 12)`,
$$

which is the CAPM of @eq-05-capm read as a prior rather than tested as a
model. Every equilibrium return sits within
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(abs(cmp5$gap_in_se)))` standard errors of the
corresponding sample mean, so the two vectors are not in conflict; they answer
different questions. The sample mean says what each market paid. The
equilibrium says what each would have to pay for investors to hold it in the
proportion they do, and it pays a beta of
`r sprintf("%.2f", cmp5$beta[cmp5$asset == "JP_equity"])` for `JP_equity` at
the market premium where the sample paid less, and revises `US_equity`, with a
beta of `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp5$beta[cmp5$asset == "US_equity"])`, down from a
sample mean the market premium does not support.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: a class-level equilibrium on a stated proxy

The application below needs $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}$ for all sixteen
classes, and eleven of them have no capitalization. What follows is a
placeholder, and it should be read as one. **Assumption:** world investable
wealth is split 40 percent equity, 40 percent government bonds, 15 percent
credit and 5 percent commodities, and within the equity, government and credit
blocks each region's share is its share of equity capitalization. Nothing in
the data supports the block split; it is a round-number stand-in for a
figure that a real allocation would take from a global market-capitalization
survey.

<!-- SS: market weights for bonds and commodities are a proxy; decide in PLAN.md open decision 3 -->

```{r}
#| label: market-weights-proxy
# ASSUMPTION, not data: the split of world wealth across the four blocks.
block <- c(equity = 0.40, government = 0.40, credit = 0.15, commodity = 0.05)
stopifnot(abs(sum(block) - 1) < 1e-12)

W16 <- matrix(0, nrow(Re), N, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Re)))
for (r in sub("_equity$", "", eq_classes)) {
  s <- W_eq[, paste0(r, "_equity")]                 # the region's share of equity capitalization
  W16[, paste0(r, "_equity")]     <- block[["equity"]]     * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_government")] <- block[["government"]] * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_credit")]     <- block[["credit"]]     * s
}
W16[, "GLOBAL_commodity"] <- block[["commodity"]]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W16) - 1) < 1e-10), identical(colnames(W16), colnames(Re)))

mkt16_e <- rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re))
delta16 <- mean(mkt16_e) / stats::var(mkt16_e)                       # @eq-06-delta
w_mkt   <- colMeans(W16)
mu_eq   <- setNames(delta16 * as.numeric(S %*% w_mkt), colnames(Re))  # @eq-06-equilibrium

c(proxy_return = mean(mkt16_e) * 12, proxy_vol = stats::sd(mkt16_e) * sqrt(12),
  proxy_sharpe = mean(mkt16_e) / stats::sd(mkt16_e) * sqrt(12), delta = delta16)

round(cbind(weight = w_mkt, sample = mu_s * 12, equilibrium = mu_eq * 12)[order(-w_mkt), ], 3)
```

A bond-heavy proxy with a Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", mean(mkt16_e) / stats::sd(mkt16_e) * sqrt(12))` at a
volatility of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * stats::sd(mkt16_e) * sqrt(12))`
implies, by @eq-06-delta, $\delta = `r sprintf("%.1f", delta16)`$, more than
twice the equity-only figure. The vector it produces disagrees with the sample
in one place that matters: `US_government` is assigned
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mu_eq[["US_government"]] * 12)` a year against a
sample mean of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mu_s[["US_government"]] * 12)`,
because it covaries negatively with the equity block and so carries almost no
risk in the market portfolio. Whether that is right depends entirely on
whether the block split is, which is what reverse optimization can and cannot
do without a market weight.
:::

### The moments as PortfolioAnalytics sees them

`PortfolioAnalytics` [@peterson2026] computes every moment an objective needs
through one function, `set.portfolio.moments()`, whose `method` argument
selects the estimator.

```{r}
#| label: moments-sample
spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

eval(formals(set.portfolio.moments)$method)

m_sample <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, spec, method = "sample")
str(m_sample, give.attr = FALSE)
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(m_sample$mu), unname(mu_s)))
```

`sample` returns the moments of @tbl-06-precision. `boudt` cleans the higher
moments through a factor structure and belongs to
@sec-11-higher-moments-theory; `black_litterman` and `meucci` blend a prior
with views and belong to @sec-17-expressing-views-theory. None of the four is
Bayes-Stein, and none accepts a market weight. The route in is the one
@sec-07-covariance-matrix-implementation used for a shrunk covariance matrix:
`optimize.portfolio()` takes a `momentFUN` argument, and a function of
`(R, portfolio, ...)` returning the named list the package expects can supply
any mean vector at all.

```{r}
#| label: momentfun
bayes_stein_moments <- function(R, portfolio, ...) {
  m <- bayes_stein(R)$mu
  S <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(R))
  list(mu = m, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = m, var = S)
}

opt_bs <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                             momentFUN = bayes_stein_moments)
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(opt_bs$moment_values$mu), unname(bs$mu)))
names(opt_bs$moment_values)
round(extractWeights(opt_bs)[extractWeights(opt_bs) > 0.005], 4)
```

The `stopifnot()` confirms that the moments the solver used are the shrunk
ones, and `maxSR = TRUE` asks for the tangency portfolio directly.

::: {.callout-important}
## On the CRAN release, `maxSR` ignores the mean you supplied

`optimize.portfolio(maxSR = TRUE)` on `PortfolioAnalytics` 2.1.2 as released
recomputes the mean from `R` inside the Sharpe-ratio search and discards the
one `momentFUN` returned, so the three estimators of this chapter would all
produce the sample-mean tangency portfolio, without a message. This book runs
on the patched build recorded in @sec-93-package-notes, and `R/_common.R`
warns if it is not installed. On the release, the portable route is the one
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation used, reading the highest Sharpe ratio
off `create.EfficientFrontier()`, which does honor `momentFUN`. Either way,
assert that the answers differ, as the application below does; a `stopifnot()`
is the only thing that distinguishes a solved problem from the wrong one
solved quietly.
:::

The package also ships the Black-Litterman formula as `black.litterman()`.
Called with the prior alone, it should return the prior, and it does, together
with a second object that needs care.

```{r}
#| label: black-litterman
bl <- black.litterman(Re, P = diag(N), Mu = mu_eq, Views = mu_eq)
str(bl, give.attr = FALSE)
c(posterior_equals_prior = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(bl$BLMu), unname(mu_eq))),
  variance_ratio = unique(round(diag(bl$BLSigma) / diag(S), 6)))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `black.litterman()` is the blending formula, not the model

Four things about this function are measured rather than documented, and a
reader who expects @black1992 will walk into each of them.

```{r}
#| label: bl-defaults
bl_default <- black.litterman(Re, P = diag(N))                   # Mu and Views left at their defaults
bl_moments <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, spec, method = "black_litterman")
c(default_view_shift_pp   = mean(as.numeric(bl_default$BLMu) - mu_s) * 1200,
  moments_shift_min_pp    = min(as.numeric(bl_moments$mu) - mu_s) * 1200,
  moments_shift_max_pp    = max(as.numeric(bl_moments$mu) - mu_s) * 1200,
  moments_variance_ratio  = min(diag(bl_moments$sigma) / diag(S)))
```

First, there is no market-weight argument and no $\delta$: `Mu` defaults to
`colMeans(R)`, so the prior is the sample mean unless @eq-06-equilibrium is
computed and passed in, as above. Second, there is no $\tau$: the prior's
uncertainty is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ itself and the view uncertainty is fixed
at $\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'$. Third, `Views = NULL`
is not the absence of a view. The default view is the standard deviation of
each view portfolio, a bullish opinion on everything, and with `P = diag(N)` it
lifts every mean by
`r sprintf("%.0f", mean(as.numeric(bl_default$BLMu) - mu_s) * 1200)` percentage
points a year on average; `set.portfolio.moments(method = "black_litterman")`
inherits this with one default view on the plain sum of the assets' returns
and shifts the means by between
`r sprintf("%.0f", min(as.numeric(bl_moments$mu) - mu_s) * 1200)` and
`r sprintf("%.0f", max(as.numeric(bl_moments$mu) - mu_s) * 1200)` points.
Fourth, `BLSigma` is the posterior covariance of the mean, not of returns: with
the prior alone it is exactly
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/`r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / unique(round(diag(bl$BLSigma) / diag(S), 6)))`$,
and `set.portfolio.moments()` hands it to the optimizer as `sigma`, which then
optimizes on half the risk. Supply `Mu` yourself, set `Views` to `P %*% Mu`
when you want the prior alone, and never let `BLSigma` reach a risk objective.
:::

One more trap, this time in how arguments travel. `set.portfolio.moments()`
recovers `Mu`, `P` and `Views` through `match.call()`, which returns the
expression a caller typed rather than its value.

```{r}
#| label: bl-matchcall
try(set.portfolio.moments(Re, spec, method = "black_litterman",
                          Mu = mu_eq, P = diag(N), Views = mu_eq))

opt_bl <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
                             momentFUN = "set.portfolio.moments",
                             method = "black_litterman",
                             Mu = mu_eq, P = diag(N), Views = mu_eq)
c(mu_honored  = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(opt_bl$moment_values$mu), unname(mu_eq))),
  sigma_ratio = unique(round(diag(opt_bl$moment_values$sigma) / diag(S), 6)))
```

Called directly with a variable, the function sees the symbol `mu_eq`, a
vector of length one, and stops. Called through `optimize.portfolio()`, which
assembles the call with `do.call()`, the values arrive intact and the mean is
honored; the covariance arrives halved, which is the fourth point of the
callout. The custom `momentFUN` of the previous chunk has neither problem, and
it is what the rest of this chapter uses.

Finally, the $\gamma/2$ convention. The equilibrium vector was built so that
the market portfolio maximizes
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\delta}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$,
and the package's quadratic utility objective puts `risk_aversion` where
$\delta/2$ stands. Feeding $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}$ back in is therefore
a test of both the vector and the convention.

```{r}
#| label: gamma-half
make_moments <- function(mu, S) {
  force(mu); force(S)
  function(R, portfolio, ...) list(mu = mu, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = mu, var = S)
}

base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

qu_weights <- function(lambda) {
  s <- base_spec |>
    add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = lambda)
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, s, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                         momentFUN = make_moments(mu_eq, S)))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

gamma_check <- c(at_delta_over_2 = max(abs(qu_weights(delta16 / 2) - w_mkt)),
                 at_delta        = max(abs(qu_weights(delta16)     - w_mkt)))
stopifnot(gamma_check[["at_delta_over_2"]] < 1e-8)
gamma_check
```

At `risk_aversion = delta16 / 2` the optimizer returns the proxy market
portfolio to within `r sprintf("%.0e", gamma_check[["at_delta_over_2"]])`; at
`risk_aversion = delta16` it returns a portfolio that differs by up to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * gamma_check[["at_delta"]])` percentage points in a
single weight. The first number is @eq-06-equilibrium working. The second is
what a reader who takes the argument's name at face value gets.

## What the Three Vectors Buy {#sec-06-expected-returns-application}

### Three tangency portfolios

The same long-only tangency problem that @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation
solved on the sample mean is now solved three times, on the sample mean, on
the Bayes-Stein vector and on the class-level equilibrium, with the sample
covariance matrix held fixed throughout so that only $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ changes.

```{r}
#| label: tangency
mus <- list(sample = mu_s, `Bayes-Stein` = bs$mu, equilibrium = mu_eq)

W3 <- sapply(mus, function(m) {
  o <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                          momentFUN = make_moments(m, S))
  w <- extractWeights(o)
  w[colnames(Re)]
})
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W3), colnames(Re)),
          !isTRUE(all.equal(W3[, "sample"], W3[, "Bayes-Stein"])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(W3[, "equilibrium"], w_mkt, tolerance = 1e-6)))

round(W3[rowSums(W3 > 0.005) > 0, ], 4)
```

The second assertion is the guard the callout asked for: the sample and
Bayes-Stein answers differ, so the supplied means were used. The third is
@eq-06-equilibrium's defining property observed: the tangency portfolio of the
equilibrium vector is the market portfolio it was read from, to solver
precision.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the long-only tangency portfolio in one quadratic program

A Sharpe ratio is invariant to the scale of the weight vector, and so is a
sign constraint. The long-only tangency portfolio can therefore be found by
minimizing variance at a unit expected return with no budget constraint, and
rescaling the answer to sum to one; this is one quadratic program rather than
a search over a frontier, and it makes the rolling exercise below cheap.

```{r}
#| label: tangency-check
tangency_lo <- function(mu, S) {
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(mu)), names(mu)))  # no long-only tangency
  N <- length(mu)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, N),
                            Amat = cbind(mu, diag(N)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, N)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), names(mu))
}

W3_qp <- sapply(mus, tangency_lo, S = S)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W3_qp), rownames(W3)), max(abs(W3 - W3_qp)) < 1e-6)
c(max_abs_difference_from_package = max(abs(W3 - W3_qp)))
```

The two routes agree to `r sprintf("%.0e", max(abs(W3 - W3_qp)))` in every
weight, which is the check that `maxSR = TRUE` on the patched build solves the
problem it is asked.
:::

```{r}
#| label: summary
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w, m = mu_s) sum(m[names(w)] * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w, m = mu_s) p_ret(w, m) / p_vol(w)
eff_bets <- function(w) 1 / sum(w^2)
turnover <- function(w1, w2) sum(abs(w1[names(w2)] - w2)) / 2

summ <- tibble::tibble(
  estimator    = names(mus),
  held         = colSums(W3 > 0.005),
  eff_bets     = apply(W3, 2, eff_bets),
  largest      = apply(W3, 2, max),
  promised_sr  = mapply(function(j, m) p_sr(W3[, j], m), seq_along(mus), mus),
  in_sample_sr = apply(W3, 2, p_sr),
  vol          = apply(W3, 2, p_vol),
  from_sample  = apply(W3, 2, function(w) turnover(W3[, "sample"], w))
)
stopifnot(identical(summ$estimator, colnames(W3)))

# The minimum-variance portfolio of chapter 9, for the comparison below.
w_gmv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(
  Re, base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"), optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_gmv <- w_gmv[colnames(Re)]
```

```{r}
#| label: summary-checks
#| include: false
# What the text reads off the table: the sample row promises most, and
# Bayes-Stein is the more concentrated of the two estimated answers, in the
# series the minimum-variance portfolio holds most of.
top <- function(w) names(which.max(w))
stopifnot(summ$estimator[which.max(summ$promised_sr)] == "sample",
          summ$estimator[which.max(summ$in_sample_sr)] == "sample",
          identical(top(W3[, "sample"]), top(W3[, "Bayes-Stein"])),
          identical(top(W3[, "sample"]), top(w_gmv)),
          max(W3[, "Bayes-Stein"]) > max(W3[, "sample"]),
          eff_bets(W3[, "Bayes-Stein"]) < eff_bets(W3[, "sample"]))

# The register of chapter 25, read as chapter 9 reads it for its out-of-sample
# table: sixteen classes, sixty-month window, monthly rebalancing, gross.
oos <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", window == 60,
                frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(oos$strategy))
oos_sr <- setNames(oos$sharpe, oos$strategy)[c("max_sharpe", "min_variance", "equal_weight")]
sr_fit <- summ$in_sample_sr[summ$estimator == "sample"]
stopifnot(!anyNA(oos_sr),
          oos_sr[["max_sharpe"]] < sr_fit,                 # the fitted figure is not earned
          names(which.min(oos_sr)) == "max_sharpe")        # and is the lowest of the three
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-06-weights
#| tbl-cap: "The three tangency portfolios. The promised Sharpe ratio is computed with the estimator's own mean vector; the in-sample Sharpe ratio with the sample mean, which is the only one the sample can score. Turnover is the share of the portfolio that must be traded to reach each answer from the sample-mean one."
#| echo: false
summ |>
  dplyr::mutate(eff_bets = sprintf("%.1f", eff_bets),
                largest = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * largest),
                dplyr::across(c(promised_sr, in_sample_sr), ~ sprintf("%.3f", .x)),
                vol = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * vol),
                from_sample = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * from_sample)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "positions held", "effective bets", "largest position",
                      "promised Sharpe", "in-sample Sharpe", "volatility",
                      "turnover from sample"))
```

```{r}
#| label: weights-frame
w_long <- as.data.frame(W3) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("asset") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-asset, names_to = "estimator", values_to = "weight") |>
  dplyr::mutate(asset = factor(asset, levels = rownames(W3)[order(W3[, "equilibrium"])]),
                estimator = factor(estimator, levels = names(mus)))
stopifnot(nrow(w_long) == 3 * N, !anyNA(w_long$weight))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-06-weights
#| fig-cap: "Weights of the long-only tangency portfolio under the three mean vectors, from one data frame. The sample and Bayes-Stein answers hold a handful of series; the equilibrium answer is the market portfolio and holds all sixteen."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.72
w_long |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(weight, asset, fill = estimator)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.72), width = 0.66) +
  scale_fill_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "weight in the long-only tangency portfolio", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

Read @tbl-06-weights across. The sample-mean portfolio holds
`r summ$held[summ$estimator == "sample"]` series with
`r sprintf("%.1f", summ$eff_bets[summ$estimator == "sample"])` effective bets
and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summ$largest[summ$estimator == "sample"])` in
`r names(which.max(W3[, "sample"]))`, and promises a Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", summ$promised_sr[summ$estimator == "sample"])`, the highest
of the three by construction, since it is scored on the vector it maximized.
The Bayes-Stein portfolio is more concentrated still, with
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summ$largest[summ$estimator == "Bayes-Stein"])` in
the same series. That is @eq-06-bs-direction at work: shrinking the means
toward $\mu_0$ mixes the tangency direction with the minimum-variance
direction, and the minimum-variance portfolio of @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation
is `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * w_gmv[["US_government"]])` `US_government`. Shrinkage did not make the portfolio more diversified. It
made it lean on the one input that is estimated well.

The equilibrium portfolio is different in kind. It holds all
`r summ$held[summ$estimator == "equilibrium"]` series with
`r sprintf("%.1f", summ$eff_bets[summ$estimator == "equilibrium"])` effective
bets, because it is the market, and its in-sample Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", summ$in_sample_sr[summ$estimator == "equilibrium"])` gives
up
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - summ$in_sample_sr[summ$estimator == "equilibrium"] / summ$in_sample_sr[summ$estimator == "sample"]))`
of the sample tangency's
`r sprintf("%.2f", sr_fit)`. That is the wrong yardstick, because the number
the sample tangency is scored on here is the one it was fitted to. @tbl-09-oos
reads the same rule out of sample from the register of
@sec-25-backtesting-application: on a sixty-month rolling window rebalanced
monthly it earns a Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", oos_sr[["max_sharpe"]])`,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * oos_sr[["max_sharpe"]] / sr_fit)` of the fitted
figure and the lowest of the three portfolios compared there. What matters
for a strategic allocation is how much each answer moves when the sample does.

### Which vector moves least

We re-estimate each of the three vectors on every rolling sixty-month window,
the window @sec-25-backtesting-application uses, and solve the same tangency
problem on each. Two things are measured: how far the mean vector itself moves
from one window to the next, and the turnover of the portfolio it implies. The
equilibrium's inputs re-estimated each window are $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and
the average market weights over the window; $\delta$ is held at its
full-sample value, because it is a preference parameter rather than a forecast
and, by the scale invariance noted above, it does not affect the tangency
weights.

```{r}
#| label: rolling
win    <- 60L
starts <- seq_len(T - win + 1L)

roll <- lapply(starts, function(s) {
  idx <- s:(s + win - 1L)
  X   <- Re[idx, ]
  Sw  <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X))
  wm  <- colMeans(W16[idx, , drop = FALSE])
  m   <- cbind(sample        = colMeans(X),
               `Bayes-Stein` = bayes_stein(X)$mu,
               equilibrium   = delta16 * as.numeric(Sw %*% wm))
  rownames(m) <- colnames(Re)
  list(mu = m, w = apply(m, 2, tangency_lo, S = Sw))
})
stopifnot(length(roll) == T - win + 1L,
          identical(rownames(roll[[1]]$w), colnames(Re)))

roll_stats <- sapply(colnames(roll[[1]]$mu), function(e) {
  MU <- sapply(roll, function(r) r$mu[, e]) * 12       # N x windows, annualized
  W  <- sapply(roll, function(r) r$w[, e])
  stopifnot(!anyNA(W))                                  # every window had a tangency
  to <- vapply(2:ncol(W), function(j) turnover(W[, j - 1], W[, j]), numeric(1))
  c(mean_abs_change_pp  = mean(abs(MU[, -1] - MU[, -ncol(MU)])) * 100,
    mean_turnover       = mean(to),
    p95_turnover        = as.numeric(quantile(to, 0.95)),
    mean_effective_bets = mean(1 / colSums(W^2)))
})

# The order the text reports, in the vectors and in the portfolios they imply.
est <- c("sample", "Bayes-Stein", "equilibrium")
stopifnot(identical(colnames(roll_stats), est),
          all(diff(roll_stats["mean_abs_change_pp", est]) < 0),
          all(diff(roll_stats["mean_turnover", est]) < 0))
to_ratio <- roll_stats["mean_turnover", c("sample", "Bayes-Stein")] /
  roll_stats["mean_turnover", "equilibrium"]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-06-rolling
#| tbl-cap: "The three estimators on rolling sixty-month windows. The first column is the mean absolute change in an annualized expected return from one window to the next, in percentage points; the turnover columns describe the tangency portfolio each vector implies."
#| echo: false
as.data.frame(t(roll_stats)) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("estimator") |>
  dplyr::mutate(mean_abs_change_pp = sprintf("%.2f", mean_abs_change_pp),
                dplyr::across(c(mean_turnover, p95_turnover), ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * .x)),
                mean_effective_bets = sprintf("%.1f", mean_effective_bets)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "mean change in an expected return (pp)", "mean turnover",
                      "95th percentile turnover", "effective bets"))
```

On `r length(roll)` windows, a sample mean moves by
`r sprintf("%.2f", roll_stats["mean_abs_change_pp", "sample"])` percentage
points a year between one window and the next, the Bayes-Stein estimate by
`r sprintf("%.2f", roll_stats["mean_abs_change_pp", "Bayes-Stein"])` and the
equilibrium return by
`r sprintf("%.2f", roll_stats["mean_abs_change_pp", "equilibrium"])`. The
tangency portfolios move accordingly: the sample-mean answer turns over
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * roll_stats["mean_turnover", "sample"])` of the
portfolio in an average month and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * roll_stats["p95_turnover", "sample"])` in the worst
twentieth, Bayes-Stein about
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - roll_stats["mean_turnover", "Bayes-Stein"] / roll_stats["mean_turnover", "sample"]))`
percent less, and the equilibrium answer
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * roll_stats["mean_turnover", "equilibrium"])`, which
is the rate at which capitalizations drift. The last row is no trick: the
tangency portfolio of @eq-06-equilibrium is the market portfolio in every
window, whatever that window's covariance matrix says, so its turnover is the
market's. The two estimated vectors move the portfolio
`r sprintf("%.0f", to_ratio[["sample"]])` and
`r sprintf("%.0f", to_ratio[["Bayes-Stein"]])` times as much as the one that
was not estimated, and @sec-23-rebalancing-application puts a price on the
difference.

### What the book carries forward

The sample mean is the input every closed form in @sec-09-mean-variance-theory
assumes and the one @tbl-06-precision shows is not known: `r n_straddle` of
`r N` intervals include zero, and the portfolio it implies is rebuilt every
month. Bayes-Stein keeps the ordering, halves the spread and cuts the
turnover, and by @eq-06-bs-direction does so by leaning on the
minimum-variance portfolio, the part of the problem
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ pins down. The equilibrium vector returns a
portfolio that is held, diversified and consistent with the covariance matrix,
and is only as good as the weights it is read from, which on this market exist
for five classes and are assumed for eleven.

The book therefore carries two of the three. Where market weights exist, the
equilibrium return of @eq-06-equilibrium is the anchor: it is the prior that
@sec-17-expressing-views-theory blends views into and the strategic policy
its tactical portfolios deviate from. Where they do not, the Bayes-Stein
estimator of @eq-06-bayes-stein is the default, because it asks nothing of the
data beyond $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ and moves
the portfolio in the direction @jagannathan2003 and @frost1988 showed a
constraint moves it anyway. The sample mean is carried as the benchmark: it is
the input whose cost @sec-08-estimation-error-theory measures and the
forecast without a signal that the predictors of
@sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-theory have to improve on.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- By @eq-06-se the precision of a mean depends on the calendar span alone, and
  on `r years` model years of data `r n_straddle` of the `r N` intervals of
  @eq-06-interval include zero. Sampling weekly instead of monthly leaves that
  unchanged and halves the standard error of the variance [@merton1980].
- A return target set on a sample mean is honored to machine precision on an
  input known to a few percentage points, and the optimizer amplifies the
  difference [@best1991; @michaud1989]. The cost is measured in
  @sec-08-estimation-error-theory.
- Bayes-Stein shrinks every mean toward the expected return of the
  minimum-variance portfolio with an intensity the data set at
  $v = `r sprintf("%.2f", bs$v)`$ here, preserves the ordering, and by
  @eq-06-bs-direction moves the tangency portfolio toward the minimum-variance
  portfolio [@jorion1986; @kan2007].
- Reverse optimization returns the vector for which the market portfolio is
  the tangency portfolio. $\delta$ scales it without changing the weights,
  and the package's `risk_aversion` is $\delta/2$, verified by feeding the
  vector back in [@sharpe1974; @black1992].
- `black.litterman()` is the blending formula only: no market weights, no
  $\tau$, a default view that is bullish on everything, and a posterior
  covariance that halves the variances. Supply `Mu` and `Views` yourself and
  keep `BLSigma` away from a risk objective.
- On rolling windows the sample tangency turns over about
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * roll_stats["mean_turnover", "sample"])` of the
  portfolio a month, Bayes-Stein
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * roll_stats["mean_turnover", "Bayes-Stein"])`,
  and the equilibrium
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * roll_stats["mean_turnover", "equilibrium"])`.
  The book carries the equilibrium as
  its anchor where market weights exist and Bayes-Stein where they do not.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Replace the target $\mu_0$ in @eq-06-bayes-stein with the plain average of
   the sixteen sample means, recompute $v$ and the long-only tangency
   portfolio, and compare it with @tbl-06-weights. Does the new target still
   move the portfolio toward the minimum-variance portfolio, and what does
   @eq-06-bs-direction say about why?
2. Reverse-optimize the five equity classes with the last month's weights,
   `W_eq[nrow(W_eq), ]`, in place of the average composition. Report how far
   each equilibrium return moves in units of the standard error in
   @tbl-06-equilibrium-equity, and say which region's revision is largest and
   why.
3. Change the block split in the worked box to 60 percent equity, 25 percent
   government, 10 percent credit and 5 percent commodities and recompute the
   class-level equilibrium. Which entries of $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}$
   move most, does the tangency portfolio still equal the proxy weights, and
   what does that say about what reverse optimization can be trusted for?
4. Recompute @tbl-06-rolling on one-hundred-and-twenty-month windows. Does the
   ranking of the three estimators change, and does the sample-mean turnover
   fall by the factor that @eq-06-se predicts for a doubled span?
